newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi king forms expanded advisory council.
newsitem.headline: Saudi king forms expanded advisory council.

text.p: Saudi Arabia on Sunday appointed an expanded 90-member Shura consultative council, dominated by technocrats, retired police and army officers and tribal leaders.
The new all-male council, which operates only as an advisory and not a legislative body, starts a four-year term on Monday.
It replaces a 60-member body which ended its term on Sunday.
The expanded Shura Council will again be headed by Saudi Islamist Sheikh Mohammad bin Jubair, a former justice minister.

The Moslem scholar has said that there were many different types of democracy in the world, stressing that grounds for comparison between a Western style democracy and the Shura system in Islam do not exist.
Royal decrees issued on Sunday showed that the new council includes 56 members with doctorate degrees, six retired senior officers, four engineers, tribal leaders and others.

Names of at least two members indicated that the country's minority Moslem Shi'ite community is represented in the new council. Conservative Saudi Arabia, which implements Sharia Islamic law, is perdominantly Sunni Moslem.
Saudi Arabia ..."is looking at broader tribal presence, involving more technocrats and maybe placating some political powers," a Riyadh-based Western diplomat said by telephone.

King Fahd on Saturday decreed the expansion of the Shura Council -- introduced in 1993 as part of promises to bring about gradual popular representation as part of long-awaited political and other reforms.

Although some government opponents see the Shura Council as a weak body which lacks broad representation, Riyadh's Western allies had welcomed the king's move to introduce such a system in a country where decision making is firmly dominated by senior members of the royal al-Saud family.
A senior Western diplomat in Riyadh said "The expansion is certainly an effort to make the council more productive, to expand its workload."
Another said "The council is aspiring for a bigger role, but in the short run, we cannot see it operating outside the prescribed parameters of economic issues."

In March 1992, King Fahd issued the Basic Law of Government organising the succession to the throne of the world's largest oil exporter and producer. He followed this up with decrees in 1993 re-organising the oil sector, limiting ministerial terms to four years and appointing the 60-man Shura council.
Kuwait is the only Gulf Arab state with an elected parliament but women cannot vote or run for public office.
